items.prompt: What three parts make up a browser 'origin'?
choices: Scheme, host, and port
Domain name and page title only
IP address and cookie value
Scheme and URL path
items.explanation: An origin is exactly the combination of scheme (http/https), host, and port — nothing about the path, query string, or page content is part of it.

items.prompt: Are `https://shop.example.com/cart` and `https://shop.example.com/checkout` the same origin?
choices: Yes — the path doesn't affect the origin at all
No — different paths always mean different origins
Only if both pages use the same HTTP method
Only if the server configures them to match
items.explanation: Origin is scheme + host + port only. Two different paths on the same host, scheme, and port are still the exact same origin.

items.prompt: Are `https://app.example.com` and `http://app.example.com` the same origin?
choices: No — the scheme differs (https vs. http)
Yes — they share the same host, so scheme doesn't matter
It depends on whether the server redirects between them
Yes, because browsers treat http and https as interchangeable
items.explanation: Scheme is one of the three required matches. https and http are different schemes, so these are different origins even with an identical host.

items.prompt: Are `https://app.example.com` and `https://app.example.com:8443` the same origin?
choices: No — the port differs (default 443 vs. explicit 8443)
Yes — ports are ignored when comparing origins
Yes, as long as the host name is identical
It depends on which one was loaded first
items.explanation: Port is part of the origin triple. `https://app.example.com` implies port 443 by default; `:8443` is a different, explicit port, so the origins don't match.

items.prompt: Are `https://app.example.com` and `https://api.example.com` the same origin?
choices: No — the host differs (app vs. api), even though the domain looks related
Yes — both are subdomains of the same example.com, so they match
Yes, because they're owned by the same company
It depends on whether they share a database
items.explanation: Host comparison is exact, not 'same registered domain' — `app` and `api` are different full hostnames, so these are different origins.

items.prompt: What is the origin of `https://shop.example.com:8080/cart?id=5`?
choices: `https://shop.example.com:8080`
`https://shop.example.com:8080/cart`
`shop.example.com`
`https://shop.example.com:8080/cart?id=5`
items.explanation: The origin is only scheme + host + port. The path (`/cart`) and query string (`?id=5`) are stripped off entirely.

items.prompt: A page served from `http://localhost:3000` calls `http://localhost:5000`. Same origin?
choices: No — the ports differ (3000 vs. 5000), even though the host and scheme match
Yes — localhost is always treated as a single trusted origin
Yes, because both are on the developer's own machine
It depends on which framework is running on each port
items.explanation: Even on localhost, the port is still part of the origin comparison — two dev servers on different ports are different origins, a common surprise for local development.

items.prompt: True or false: if two URLs resolve to the same origin, a request between them is cross-origin.
choices: False — same origin means it's NOT cross-origin at all
True — any two different URLs are always cross-origin
True, unless the request uses GET
False, but only when cookies aren't involved
items.explanation: "Cross-origin" specifically means the origins differ. If scheme, host, and port all match, the request is same-origin and none of the CORS machinery even applies.

items.prompt: What exactly determines whether two URLs share the same origin?
choices: Scheme, host, and port must all match exactly
Only the host needs to match
The registered domain (e.g. example.com) must match, subdomains included
Origins are determined by the server's CORS configuration, not the URL
items.explanation: All three — scheme, host, and port — must match. Any single mismatch makes the URLs cross-origin, regardless of how related the domains look.
items.reference:
Origin = scheme + host + port
🔗 Path and query string are NOT part of it
⚠️ A single mismatch in any of the three makes it cross-origin
Why: this triple is exactly what the browser compares before deciding whether a request is cross-origin at all.
items.reflection: Origin boundaries aren't unique to browsers — mobile apps, desktop apps with plugin systems, and even OS-level sandboxing all draw a similar line between 'my own code and data' and 'someone else's.' Where else have you seen a system defined by a strict identity triple like this, rather than a looser notion of 'basically the same place'?

choices: Neither — for origin purposes they're different (host differs: blog vs. shop), regardless of shared ownership or domain
They're the same, because they share the registered domain company.com
It depends on whether both use HTTPS
It depends on whether they're hosted on the same physical server
items.explanation: Browsers compare the full host string exactly, not the registered domain. Shared ownership, shared infrastructure, and a shared root domain are all irrelevant — `blog` and `shop` are different hosts, full stop.

items.prompt: A page at `https://app.example.com` redirects internally from `/old-path` to `/new-path`, still on the same host, scheme, and port. Does this redirect involve a cross-origin boundary?
choices: No — only the path changed, and path isn't part of the origin
Yes — any redirect counts as crossing origins
Yes, because redirects always go through a new TCP connection
It depends on whether the redirect uses a 301 or 302 status
items.explanation: A path-only change never crosses an origin boundary, no matter how the navigation happens. Origin is indifferent to path, query string, and redirect mechanics — only scheme/host/port matter.

items.prompt: What does the same-origin policy restrict?
choices: Whether JavaScript running on one origin can read a response from a different origin
Whether a server is allowed to receive requests from other servers
Whether a browser can open more than one tab at once
Whether HTTPS traffic can be inspected by a proxy
items.explanation: It's specifically about JavaScript reading cross-origin responses — not about servers receiving requests, which they can always do.

items.prompt: Does Postman enforce the same-origin policy?
choices: No — it's a browser-enforced rule; Postman and curl don't apply it at all
Yes — Postman enforces an identical policy to browsers
Only when testing against production servers
Only if the 'strict mode' setting is enabled
items.explanation: The same-origin policy lives entirely in the browser's JavaScript engine. Tools that just send HTTP requests, like Postman or curl, have no such restriction.

items.prompt: A browser page's fetch() call reaches the server, which responds with 200 and valid data — but the browser still won't let the page's JavaScript read it. What's the most likely explanation?
choices: The browser is enforcing the same-origin policy and the server didn't opt in via CORS
The server's response body was corrupted in transit
The browser ran out of memory
The request used the wrong HTTP method
items.explanation: A successful server response that JavaScript still can't read is the textbook signature of same-origin enforcement — the server did its job, the browser is the one refusing to hand the data over.

items.prompt: Who decides whether a page's JavaScript gets to see a cross-origin response?
choices: The browser, based on whether the server opted in via CORS headers
The operating system's firewall
The server alone, by choosing not to respond
The page's own JavaScript code, via a permissions check
items.explanation: The browser is the enforcer. It checks the server's CORS headers on the response and then decides, unilaterally, whether to expose that response to the page's script.

items.prompt: Does the same-origin policy prevent a server from processing a cross-origin request?
choices: No — the server can process it and respond normally; the restriction is only on the browser handing the response to JavaScript
Yes — the server refuses to process any cross-origin request
Yes, but only for POST requests
It depends on the server's operating system
items.explanation: Server-side processing is completely unaffected by the same-origin policy — it's a browser-side read restriction, not a request-blocking mechanism on the server.

items.prompt: Why might server logs show a successful request while the browser console shows an error for the exact same call?
choices: Because the browser's same-origin enforcement happens after the server already responded successfully
Because the server logs are simply wrong
Because the browser retried the request and only the retry failed
Because server logs never record failed requests
items.explanation: The server-side success and the browser-side failure are two separate, sequential events — the server finishes first, then the browser evaluates whether to expose the result, and can say no.

items.prompt: Is the same-origin policy 'on' by default, or does a server have to request it?
choices: It's on by default for cross-origin reads; a server has to opt OUT of the restriction via CORS headers, not into it
It's off by default; a server has to opt in to enable it
It only activates once a site has more than one subdomain
It's controlled entirely by the client's operating system settings
items.explanation: The restriction is the default behavior. CORS headers are how a server grants an exception to that default, not how it turns the restriction on.

items.prompt: A page can always freely read responses from requests it sends to...
choices: Its own origin
Any origin, as long as the response is JSON
Any origin that uses HTTPS
Any origin whose server is publicly reachable
items.explanation: Same-origin requests are never restricted by this policy at all — the whole mechanism only exists to govern cross-origin reads.

items.prompt: What does the same-origin policy actually restrict, and who enforces it?
choices: It restricts JavaScript from reading cross-origin responses, enforced entirely by the browser
It restricts servers from accepting requests from unknown clients, enforced by the server
It restricts DNS resolution across different top-level domains, enforced by the resolver
It restricts which ports a browser is allowed to connect to, enforced by the operating system
items.explanation: This is a browser-side read restriction on JavaScript, not a network-level or server-level restriction — the server can always receive and answer the request.
items.reference:
Same-origin policy
🌐 Own origin: always readable
🚫 Other origin: blocked by default, enforced by the browser
Why: the server still answers — only whether JavaScript gets to read that answer is in question.
items.reflection: A default-deny posture that requires an explicit opt-in shows up far beyond browsers — firewall rules, API gateway allowlists, and permission systems on phones all default to blocking and require something to actively grant access. Where have you seen a 'default deny, explicit opt-in' pattern used instead of the opposite, and why might a system choose one over the other?

items.prompt: A QA engineer tests an endpoint with curl, sees a clean 200 response, and concludes 'the frontend bug must be somewhere else, since the API clearly works.' What's the gap in that reasoning?
choices: curl doesn't enforce the same-origin policy at all, so a working curl test says nothing about whether a browser's JavaScript would be allowed to read the same response
curl and browsers always behave identically, so the reasoning is correct
curl only fails when the server returns an error status, so a 200 always proves the frontend works too
The gap is that curl uses a different HTTP version than browsers
items.explanation: curl bypasses same-origin entirely. A clean curl response only proves the server half of the system works — it says nothing about whether the browser will let JavaScript see that same response.

items.prompt: If a page's own backend (same origin) is temporarily down and returns no response at all, is that a same-origin-policy failure?
choices: No — same-origin requests are never restricted by this policy; a down server is an unrelated network/availability failure
Yes — any failed request from a page is a same-origin-policy failure by definition
Yes, because the browser always applies the same-origin policy to every request regardless of origin
It depends on whether the backend uses HTTPS
items.explanation: This policy only ever restricts *cross*-origin reads. A same-origin request that fails because the server is down is a plain availability problem, with the policy never entering the picture.

items.prompt: Does fetch()'s promise reject when the server responds with a 404?
choices: No — it resolves normally, with response.ok set to false
Yes — any non-2xx status rejects the promise
Only if the response body is empty
Only in strict mode
items.explanation: fetch() treats any completed HTTP response, even an error one, as a resolved promise. Rejection is reserved for network-level failures.

items.prompt: What kind of failure DOES cause fetch()'s promise to reject?
choices: Network-level failures, like being blocked by CORS or losing connectivity
Any response with a status code 400 or above
Any response larger than 1MB
Any response missing a Content-Type header
items.explanation: Rejection is specifically for cases where no usable HTTP response exists at all — a CORS block or a network failure, not an error status that the server did manage to send.

items.prompt: Will a plain try/catch around `await fetch(...)` catch a 500 Internal Server Error?
choices: No — a 500 resolves the promise just like a 200 does; try/catch has nothing to catch
Yes — try/catch catches every kind of HTTP failure
Yes, but only in async functions declared with 'use strict'
It depends on the server's framework
items.explanation: A 500 is still a completed HTTP response from fetch()'s point of view, so the promise resolves. try/catch only intercepts thrown errors or rejected promises — this isn't one.

items.prompt: What's the explicit check needed to detect an HTTP error status after a successful fetch() resolution?
choices: Checking response.ok (or response.status) directly
Wrapping the fetch() call in a second try/catch
Checking whether response is null
Checking the response's Content-Length header
items.explanation: response.ok (true only for 2xx) is exactly the signal try/catch can't give you — it has to be read explicitly after the promise resolves.

items.prompt: A page's fetch() call gets blocked by CORS. Does the promise resolve or reject?
choices: Reject — a CORS block is treated as a network-level failure
Resolve, with response.ok set to false
Resolve, with a status code of 0
Neither — the call throws synchronously before returning a promise
items.explanation: CORS blocks fall under 'no usable response reached JavaScript,' which is exactly the network-failure category that rejects the promise.

items.prompt: From inside a try/catch, can you tell a CORS block apart from a plain network outage just by catching the error?
choices: No — both land in the catch block the same way; fetch() doesn't distinguish them for you
Yes — CORS errors always have a distinct error.name property
Yes — CORS errors always include the blocked origin's name in the message
Yes, because CORS errors are caught by a separate, dedicated handler
items.explanation: Both are network-level rejections from fetch()'s perspective and look alike to a generic catch block — the browser's console may show more detail, but the caught error itself doesn't cleanly separate the two.

items.prompt: True or false: 'the promise resolved' means 'the request succeeded.'
choices: False — resolved just means a response object exists; it could still carry a 404 or 500
True — resolution and success always mean the same thing for fetch()
True, as long as the response has a body
False, because resolved promises never carry status information
items.explanation: Resolution only means fetch() got a response to hand back, good or bad. 'Success' is a separate judgment that requires checking response.ok.

items.prompt: Why does this distinction 'trip up a lot of try/catch code,' according to L1?
choices: Because developers assume try/catch alone catches all API failures, when it only catches network-level failures
Because try/catch doesn't exist in older browsers
Because fetch() doesn't support async/await
Because the distinction only applies to POST requests
items.explanation: The common mistake is treating try/catch as a complete safety net for fetch() — it only covers the rejection path, leaving HTTP error statuses to slip through silently.

items.prompt: What's the fundamental difference between how fetch() handles an HTTP error status versus a network-level failure?
choices: An HTTP error status resolves the promise (with response.ok false); a network-level failure (including CORS) rejects it
Both reject the promise, but with different error messages
Both resolve the promise, but with different status codes
An HTTP error status throws synchronously, before any promise is created
items.explanation: This is the core distinction the whole unit turns on: resolution vs. rejection maps to 'did a response exist' — not to 'was the response good.'
items.reference:
fetch() resolve vs. reject
✅ 404 / 500 → resolves, response.ok is false
❌ CORS block / network failure → rejects
Why: try/catch only ever sees the reject side — the resolve side needs an explicit response.ok check.
items.reflection: Separating 'the operation completed' from 'the operation succeeded' is a distinction that shows up well beyond fetch() — a database query that returns zero rows isn't an error, a shell command that exits with a non-zero code didn't crash, and a form submission that comes back with validation errors still got a response. Where else have you seen 'it returned' and 'it worked' get conflated, with real consequences?

items.prompt: A developer writes `try { const r = await fetch(url); return r.json(); } catch { showError(); }` and ships it. A 404 comes back from the API. What happens?
choices: No error is shown — the try block runs to completion, parses the error body as JSON, and returns it as if it were valid data
showError() runs, because the catch block intercepts the 404
The function throws a TypeError before reaching the catch block
The browser automatically retries the request on any 4xx status
items.explanation: fetch() resolved, so the try block keeps going — it calls .json() on whatever body came back and returns it, silently treating a 404's error payload as if it were successful data. Nothing here ever throws.

items.prompt: Would wrapping the same fetch() call in a second, nested try/catch fix the 404-swallowing problem from the previous question?
choices: No — nesting try/catch doesn't help; nothing in the resolve path throws, so there's still nothing for either catch block to intercept
Yes — a nested try/catch always catches what the outer one misses
Yes, as long as the inner catch block calls response.json() instead of the outer one
It depends on whether the nested block is declared async
items.explanation: Adding more catch blocks doesn't create a throw where none exists. The fix has to be inside the try block itself — explicitly checking response.ok and throwing when it's false — not adding more layers of catching.

items.prompt: What does CORS stand for?
choices: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
Client-Origin Request Security
Cross-Origin Request Standard
Cached Origin Response System
items.explanation: CORS is Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — the mechanism that lets a server share its resources with origins other than its own.

items.prompt: How does a server actually use CORS to opt in to cross-origin access?
choices: By sending specific response headers that the browser checks
By installing a CORS certificate alongside its TLS certificate
By whitelisting IP addresses at the firewall level
By running a separate CORS-only server process
items.explanation: CORS is entirely header-based — the server's response carries headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin that the browser inspects before deciding what JavaScript gets to see.

items.prompt: Without any CORS headers at all, what's the default for a cross-origin request?
choices: Blocked from JavaScript's view — CORS headers are what override that default
Allowed by default — CORS headers are only needed to restrict access further
It depends on whether the request uses HTTP or HTTPS
Allowed for GET, blocked for everything else, with no headers needed
items.explanation: The same-origin policy's default is 'blocked.' CORS headers exist specifically to opt back in to cross-origin access — there's no default-allow state to restrict from.

items.prompt: Who checks the CORS headers on a response before data reaches JavaScript?
choices: The browser
The server that sent the response
A third-party CDN
The page's own JavaScript code
items.explanation: The browser is both the sender of the request and the gatekeeper evaluating the response's CORS headers — the server just states what it allows.

items.prompt: If a server never sends any Access-Control-* headers, can its API still be called successfully by curl?
choices: Yes — curl doesn't look at CORS headers at all, so the request and response proceed normally
No — the server will refuse to respond without CORS headers present
No, curl requires CORS headers to parse the response body
It depends on the HTTP version used
items.explanation: CORS headers are irrelevant outside a browser context. curl has no same-origin policy to satisfy in the first place, so missing headers change nothing for it.

items.prompt: Is CORS a client-side setting, a server-side setting, or both?
choices: Server-side — the server sends the headers; the browser just reads and enforces what they say
Client-side only — a setting in the browser's own preferences
Neither — it's configured at the DNS level
Both equally — the client and server each send separate CORS headers
items.explanation: The server controls what CORS allows by setting response headers; the browser's role is reading and enforcing those headers, not configuring them.

items.prompt: What's the relationship between CORS and the same-origin policy?
choices: CORS is the mechanism a server uses to relax the browser's default same-origin restriction
They're unrelated, separately-enforced browser features
CORS replaces the same-origin policy entirely in modern browsers
The same-origin policy is a subset of CORS, not the other way around
items.explanation: Same-origin policy sets the default (blocked); CORS is specifically the opt-in path a server uses to grant exceptions to that default.

items.prompt: Does a browser need any special configuration from the user to respect a server's CORS headers?
choices: No — CORS enforcement is a built-in, always-on browser behavior
Yes — the user must enable a 'strict CORS' browser flag
Yes — each site must be manually added to an allowlist by the user
Only in incognito/private browsing mode
items.explanation: CORS enforcement isn't optional or user-configurable — every modern browser applies it automatically to every cross-origin request.

items.prompt: What mechanism does CORS provide, and how does a server actually use it?
choices: CORS is a header-based opt-in: the server sends response headers naming which origins may read the response, and the browser enforces them
CORS is a protocol-level flag set during the TLS handshake
CORS is a DNS record that whitelists allowed callers
CORS is a cookie that the server sets on the first request
items.explanation: CORS lives entirely in HTTP response headers, checked by the browser — nothing about TLS, DNS, or cookies is involved in the actual opt-in mechanism.
items.reference:
CORS
🔓 Server opts in via response headers
👀 Browser checks before handing data to JS
Why: CORS is what lets a server override the same-origin default.
items.reflection: A resource owner stating, via metadata rather than a conversation, who else is allowed to read something is a pattern that shows up in file permissions, API scopes, and even email sharing settings. Where else have you seen 'who may access this' expressed as attached metadata the requester's own tool then has to respect?

items.prompt: A server team says 'we don't need to add CORS headers, our API already requires an API key for every request.' Does an API key substitute for CORS headers in letting a browser page read the response?
choices: No — an API key controls who can call the server; CORS headers control whether the browser lets JavaScript read the result. They solve different problems
Yes — any authentication mechanism automatically satisfies CORS
Yes, as long as the API key is sent as a header rather than a query parameter
It depends on whether the API key is validated before or after the response is sent
items.explanation: Authentication and CORS are orthogonal. A request can be perfectly authenticated and still get its response blocked from JavaScript if the server never sends the right CORS headers.

choices: No — Postman never enforces CORS to begin with, so its success says nothing about whether a browser would allow JavaScript to read the same response
Yes — if Postman can read it, any client can read it
Yes, because Postman and browsers use the same underlying HTTP engine
It depends on whether Postman was run in 'browser simulation' mode
items.explanation: Postman's success is uninformative here precisely because it never checks CORS headers. A working Postman call and a working browser call are testing two different things.

items.prompt: What HTTP method does a browser's preflight request use?
choices: OPTIONS
GET
HEAD
CHECK
items.explanation: The browser automatically sends an OPTIONS request as the preflight — it's a dedicated method for exactly this 'would you allow this?' question.

items.prompt: When does a preflight request happen, relative to the real request?
choices: Before — it's an automatic check sent first, asking permission for the real request
After — it confirms the real request already succeeded
Simultaneously, in parallel with the real request
Only after the real request has already failed once
items.explanation: A preflight is strictly a before-the-fact check. If it's rejected, the real request is never sent at all.

items.prompt: What does the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header tell the browser?
choices: Which origins are allowed to read the response
Which origins are allowed to send requests to the server at all
How long the response should be cached
Which encryption algorithm the response uses
items.explanation: It's purely a 'who may read this' signal to the browser — it doesn't control whether the server accepts the request, only whether the browser hands over the answer.

items.prompt: Is a preflight request initiated by JavaScript code, or automatically by the browser?
choices: Automatically by the browser — JavaScript never explicitly triggers it
By JavaScript, via a separate preflight() API call
By the server, as a response to the first failed request
By a browser extension, if one is installed
items.explanation: The browser decides on its own, based on the request's properties, whether a preflight is needed — there's no JavaScript API for triggering it manually.

items.prompt: What question is a preflight request essentially asking the server?
choices: 'Would you allow this specific request, if I sent it?'
'Are you currently online?'
'What is your server's software version?'
'How many requests have you received today?'
'Can you compress this response?'
items.explanation: It's a permission check — the browser describing the real request it wants to make and asking whether that would be allowed.

items.prompt: If a server's preflight response doesn't list the calling origin, what happens to the real request?
choices: It's never sent at all
It's sent anyway, but the response is discarded
It's sent with a warning header attached
It's sent, but with the Authorization header stripped
items.explanation: A failed preflight stops things before the real request exists on the wire — the browser doesn't send-then-discard, it simply never sends it.

items.prompt: True or false: every cross-origin request involves a preflight.
choices: False — only requests outside the narrow 'simple request' definition need one
True — all cross-origin requests are preflighted without exception
True, but only for requests with a request body

None — preflight is decided by a separate, fourth factor

items.prompt: Server logs show a successful GET, but the console still says CORS. Did the real request reach the server?

No — a CORS error always means the request never arrived

Only if the request used HTTPS

items.prompt: Server logs show a 404, with no CORS console error at all. What does fetch() do?
choices: It resolves; response.ok is false
It rejects, just like a CORS block
It throws synchronously
It retries automatically

items.prompt: No server logs at all, no CORS console details, and the network is offline. What's the likely cause?
choices: A plain network failure, unrelated to CORS

A blocked simple-request response

A 404, and a 500

items.prompt: What does the Access-Control-Max-Age header control?
choices: How long the browser may reuse a preflight's approval before asking again

The maximum age of cached response data
The timeout before a request is considered failed

choices: Close to every one pays the extra preflight round-trip
Only the first one ever gets a preflight

A 200 status code is enough, regardless of headers

items.prompt: If the preflight is rejected, does the real GET /users request still get sent, just with its response ignored?

It depends on the browser vendor
items.explanation: Rejection stops the process entirely before the real request exists — there's no send-then-discard behavior.

items.prompt: Is the preflight's cached approval scoped per method/headers combination and resource, or is it a blanket approval for the whole origin?

It's scoped per browser tab, regardless of method or resource

items.prompt: Walking through the preflight round-trip: what does the browser send first, what does it check in the response, and what happens if that check fails?

items.prompt: For a simple request that the browser ends up blocking, did the server ever see the request?

items.prompt: Does this 'blocked later' scenario explain why server logs can show success while the browser console shows a CORS failure?

items.prompt: Is a preflight involved at all in the 'simple request blocked later' scenario?

items.prompt: For a simple GET request to a misconfigured server, at what point does the failure actually happen?

Before the request is sent, identical to a preflight failure
During the TCP handshake
During DNS resolution

items.prompt: Why can't a developer rely on 'no preflight in the network tab' to mean 'CORS isn't the problem'?

Because the network tab never shows preflight requests even when they happen
